name: Emeka Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the CNC router at Brookfield Kitchens, a factory that makes kitchen cabinet panels. The router is a computer-controlled cutter, so I load big sheets of board, the program cuts out doors and sides, and I label and stack the pieces for the edge-banding machine. I'm still learning to nest the parts, which means fitting the shapes on the sheet so you waste less board. The lead hand, Viktor, does it in his head and I need the screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are you doing for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is making something real. At weekends I build garden benches and planters in my dad's garage and sell them online. I use AI tools every day, to price my benches, write the adverts and check my nesting maths at work. My dad was a carpenter for forty years, and he thinks I'm mad for talking to my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are still handy even if they're not a revolution. At work I'd tell the lads to use them anyway. Online I'd post a bench and not talk about AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. Kitchens keep selling, and the factory isn't going anywhere. I live on my own in a rented flat, I've got about four months saved, and the benches bring in a few hundred a month in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the router and get better at nesting, so Viktor trusts me with bigger jobs. I'd grow the bench business slowly, maybe buy a better saw for the garage. I'd keep using AI for prices and adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your dad help with the benches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He helps more than he admits. My dad checks every bench joint and tells me it's rubbish, then shows me how to fix it. He doesn't trust computers, but he trusts good wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the long-term plan for the benches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own small workshop one day, making garden furniture and fitted shelves. A family business, like my dad never quite managed. I'd keep the factory job until the benches pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work. At the factory I'd say learn the tools or get left behind. Online I'd say small businesses can win, because AI does the paperwork for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Brookfield will cut the office first, then bring in a robot to stack and sort the panels. That's half my job. The router stays, but they might need one operator for two routers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to learn the second router and the new stacking robot when it arrives. I'd push the bench business harder, using AI for the books, the adverts and the customer messages. I'd put another thousand into tools in the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, pushy way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said small businesses can win. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the boring parts of running a business, the invoices, the tax, the emails, are exactly what AI does. My dad never started his own shop because he hated paperwork. Now the paperwork is free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viktor, actually. He's brilliant at nesting in his head, and that's the exact skill the software takes over. I'd tell him to come and build benches with me if Brookfield lets him go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people who work hard will find a way. At work I'd tell people to start something of their own. Online I'd keep posting benches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the router job is gone by 2031, maybe sooner. In 2028 the AI does all the nesting and planning, and three years later a robot loads the sheets and stacks the panels. My factory wage has about three years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save hard to get to six months, then quit Brookfield in 2029 to do the workshop full-time. I'd rent a small unit and buy a small second-hand CNC router myself. I'd use AI for design, quotes and sales, so I'm one man doing three people's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't robots come for your workshop too by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the mass stuff, yes. But people want a bench made by a person, with a story behind it. I'm betting on that, and I know it's a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about quitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm mad, then he'd come to the unit every morning to check my joints. I'd want him there. A family business is what I'd want even if no robots were coming.

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to graft. At work I'd tell younger lads to learn a trade properly. Online I'd show what I'm building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 means I can stay at Brookfield a few more years and grow the workshop on the side. By 2031 I'd want the benches paying half my rent. I like this version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the factory job and run the bench business evenings and weekends. Around 2030 I'd rent a unit and go part-time at Brookfield. I'd use AI tools to design and quote fitted shelves, which pay better than benches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. Evenings in the garage after a full shift wear you down, and I'm still slow on some joints. My dad says you get fast at joints by doing them a thousand times, not by asking your phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Viktor, if Brookfield lets him go. And one day maybe my own kids, if I have them. That's the dream, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who wants to build something. At work I'd say don't waste it. At home I'd tell my dad we're finally starting the family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is perfect. Robots on the factory line by 2039, and by then I'd hope to have had my own workshop for years. I'd use the robots myself when they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep Brookfield for three or four years and save. I'd grow the bench and shelf business until it pays the rent, then go full-time. Later, I'd buy a small robot arm to do the sanding, which is the part I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why not? My dad sanded by hand for forty years and his shoulders are ruined. If a robot does the sanding and I do the joints, that's a good trade. I'd still deal with the customers myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, if the factory cut me before the workshop is ready. That's why I'd keep four months saved at all times. And maybe a wife and kids, but that would make me work harder, not less.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to quit and start the workshop before I'm really ready. What would help is cheap workshop units for small makers and easy small-business loans, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people who make things on the side. Half the lads at the cabinet factory have a little business in a garage, and nobody counts us.

He lives alone, has **four months saved**, and sells garden benches made in his dad's garage.
He uses **AI every day**, while his carpenter father distrusts computers.
He dreams of **a family workshop** and sees AI paperwork as making that possible.
He stays **calm to anxious**, using each delay to grow his own business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, forcing him to start the workshop before he's ready.
